passages.original: Quibus quomodo possit om- nium animalium descriptio coaptari, tentabimus suo loco dicere. Alii vero qui philosophorum stul- tam sequuntur sapientiam, duo hemisphaeria in duobus templi Cherubim, nos et Antipodas, quasi supinos et cadentes homines suspicantur· Plerique, juxta Platonem, rationale animae, et irascitivum, et concupiscitivum, quod ille λογικήν βίΟυμικδνβΙέπ’.- Ουμητικ&ν vocat, ad hominem, et leonem ac vitulum referunt : rationem et cognitionem, et mentem, et consilium, eamdemque virtutem atque sapientiam in cerebri arce ponentes : feritatem vero et ira- cundiam atque violentiam in leone, quae consi- stat in felle.
passages.english: How the description of all the living creatures can be fitted to these, we shall try to say in its proper place. Others, who follow the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, suppose that the two hemispheres are [meant] by the two Cherubim of the temple, we and the Antipodes, men as it were lying on their backs and falling. Many, following Plato, refer the rational, the irascible and the concupiscible [parts] of the soul, which he calls *logikon*, *thymikon* and *epithymētikon*, to the man, the lion and the calf: placing reason and knowledge, and mind and counsel, and likewise virtue and wisdom, in the citadel of the brain; but ferocity, wrath and violence in the lion, which resides in the gall.
passages.notes: The Greek terms are garbled by the scan ("λογικήν βίΟυμικδνβΙέπ’.- Ουμητικ&ν"); read as λογικόν, θυμικόν, ἐπιθυμητικόν.

passages.original: Hanc igitur qua- drigam in aurigae modum Deus regit, et incompo- sitis currentem gradibus refrenat, docilemque fa- cit, et suo parere cogit imperio. Quam disputatio- nem partium animae, id est hominis, qui minor mundus ab iisdem philosophis appellatur, etiam nos attingemus. Sunt qui simpliciter in quatuor animalibus, juxta Hippocratis sententiam, quatuor arbitrantur elementa mundi monstrari, de quibus constant omnia : ignem, aerem, aquam, terram. Quae quomodo sibi misceantur, et cum singula sint, sibi juncta videantur, invicemque se tangant, et in una persona animantium quatuor species habeant ac figuras, non est propositi operis.
passages.english: This four-horse team, then, God steers like a charioteer, reins it in when it runs with disordered steps, makes it tractable, and compels it to obey his command. This discussion of the parts of the soul, that is, of man, whom the same philosophers call a lesser world, we too shall touch upon. There are some who simply think that in the four living creatures, following the opinion of Hippocrates, the four elements of the world are shown, of which all things consist: fire, air, water, earth. How these are mixed with one another, and how, though each is distinct, they appear joined to one another and touch one another, and have in the one person of the living creatures four kinds and shapes, is not the purpose of the present work.

passages.original: Scintillas rutilantes, cuncta ple- na luminis indicare, et manus hominis sub pennis tam ipsius hominis, quam leonis, et vituli, et aquilae : ut ratio cuncta sustentet, ac de humili- tate terrena ad coelestia sublevet. Haec et ad Evan- gelia et ad cuncta quae supra posuimus referre possumus. Audisse me memini quatuor perturba- tiones, de quibus plenissime Cicero in Tusculanis disputat, gaudii, aegritudinis, cupidinis et timoris, quorum duo praesentia, duo futura sunt, per qua- tuor significari animalia, de quibus et Virgilius breviter (AEneid. lib. VI) :
passages.english: [They say that] the glittering sparks indicate that all things are full of light, and [that] the hands of a man [are] under the wings both of the man himself and of the lion, the calf and the eagle: so that reason sustains all things and lifts them from earthly lowliness to heavenly things. These things we can refer both to the Gospels and to all that we have set out above. I remember hearing that the four perturbations, which Cicero discusses most fully in the Tusculans—joy, grief, desire and fear, of which two are present and two future—are signified by the four living creatures, of which Virgil too [speaks] briefly (Aeneid book VI):
passages.notes: The quotation itself follows outside the passage.

passages.original: » Non solum idolum Zeli stabat in introitu portae Aquilonis, sed et omnes templi parietes diversis idolorum imaginibus pin- gebantur : ut nulla esset 86 bestia, quam non parietis pictura monstraret. Hoc in delubris ido- lorum, fanisque gentilium hucusque perspicimus, quod omnia genera bestiarum adoret stulta religio. Unde et Virgilius ait :
passages.english: Not only did the idol of jealousy stand at the entrance of the north gate, but all the walls of the temple were also painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast which the painting on the wall did not display. This we see even now in the shrines of idols and the temples of the gentiles, that a foolish religion worships every kind of beast. Hence Virgil also says:
passages.notes: The stray "86" is a page number from the edition, omitted.

passages.original: Quodque dicit : Ascendit gloria de medio civitatis, aliis verbis loquitur Domi- nus ad discipulos : Surgite, abeamus hinc (Joan. XIV, 31). Et ad Judaeos : Relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta (Matth. XXIII, 38). Josephus quoque refert 1 auditam vocem in templo angelorum et fortitudi- num coelestium, quae prius in urbis praesidio erant : Abeamus ex his sedibus (Joseph. Antiq. Jud.). Mi- rumque in modum usque in praesentem diem glo- ria Domini, quae deseruit templum, stat super mon- tem Oliveti, et in crucis signo rutilans, spectat templum quondam Judaicum, in favillas et cineres dissolutum.
passages.english: And as for its saying, "The glory went up from the midst of the city," in other words the Lord says to the disciples, "Rise, let us go hence" (John 14:31). And to the Jews: "Your house will be left to you desolate" (Matt. 23:38). Josephus too relates that a voice was heard in the temple, of the angels and heavenly powers who had formerly been the city's guard: "Let us depart from these seats" (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities). And in a marvellous way, up to the present day, the glory of the Lord, which deserted the temple, stands on the Mount of Olives and, gleaming in the sign of the cross, looks upon the once Jewish temple, reduced to embers and ashes.
passages.notes: The passage Jerome cites is actually in Josephus' Jewish War, not the Antiquities.

passages.original: (Vers. 10.) « Persae et Lydi [Vulg. Lydia] et Libyes erant in exercitu tuo, viri bellatores tui : clypeum et galeam suspenderunt in te pro ornatu tuo (sive peltas et galeas suspenderunt in te, ipsi dederunt gloriam tuam). » Persas fuisse fortissimos, quorum rex Cyrus, ut Isaiae vaticinio praedicatur (Isa. XLV), subverso Astyage, rege Medorum, Baby- lonem ceperit, et sacra, et saecularis narrat historia. Lydos quoque illo tempore inter gentes robustissi- mas reputatos, quorum rex Croesus ab eodem Cyro captus sit, Xenophon scribit plenissime. Et Libyas cum Troglodytis et AEthiopibus venisse contra Jerusalem, in Paralipomenon volumine legimus (II Paral. XII) : qui quia illis temporibus florentis- simi erant, famosi ad praelia pugnatores.
passages.english: (Verse 10.) "Persians and Lydians [Vulgate: Lydia] and Libyans were in your army, your men of war: they hung up shield and helmet in you for your adornment (or: they hung up targes and helmets in you; they gave you your glory)." That the Persians were most valiant, whose king Cyrus, as is foretold in the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa. 45), overthrew Astyages king of the Medes and took Babylon, both sacred and secular history relate. That the Lydians too were reckoned at that time among the most powerful nations, whose king Croesus was captured by the same Cyrus, Xenophon writes most fully. And that the Libyans came against Jerusalem with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians we read in the volume of Chronicles (2 Chron. 12): since they were most flourishing in those times, [they were] famous fighters in battle.

passages.original: Quod quidem dicunt sub Nabuchodonosor esse com- pletum : alii sub Cambyse filio Cyri, qui AEgyptum usque ad AEthiopiam vastavit, ita ut Apim interfi- ceret, et omnia illorum simulacra deleret. Quam ob causam putant eum versum in amentiam casu equi, et proprio pugione confossum. Plenissime hanc historiam narrat Herodotus : ubi et omnis AEgyptus per pagos et castella et vicos describitur, et Nili origo gentisque illius populi, et mensura terrae per circuitum usque ad desertum AEthiopiae et littora Magni maris, Libyaeque et Arabiae confi- nia demonstrantur.
passages.english: This, indeed, they say was fulfilled under Nebuchadnezzar; others [say] under Cambyses son of Cyrus, who laid waste Egypt as far as Ethiopia, so that he killed Apis and destroyed all their images. For this reason they think he was driven to madness, and by a fall from his horse was pierced by his own dagger. Herodotus narrates this history most fully: where all Egypt is also described by districts, forts and villages, and the source of the Nile and [the origin] of that people, and the measurement of the land around as far as the desert of Ethiopia and the shores of the Great Sea, and the borders of Libya and Arabia are set out.
passages.notes: "gentisque illius populi" is awkward; perhaps "origin of that nation".

passages.original: Igitur Judaei et nostri judaizantes putant Gog gentes esse Scythicas 4 immanes et innumerabiles, quae trans Caucasum montem, et Maeotidem paludem, et prope Caspium mare ad Indiam usque tendantur; et has post mille annorum regnum esse diabolo commovendas, quae veniant in terram Israel, ut pugnent contra sanctos, multis secum gentibus congregatis. Pri- mum, Mosoch, quos Josephus interpretatur Cap- padocas, deinde Thubal, quos idem Iberos, vel Hispanos, Hebraei Italos Suspicantur, habentes se- cum in exercitu Persas, AEthiopas, et Libyas : Go- mer quoque et Thogorma, quos Galatas et Phrygas interpretantur : Sabaeos quoque et Dedan, et Car- thaginenses, sive Tharsis, et hoc est, quod Joannes quoque in sua ponit Apocalypsi : Et cum finiti fue- rint mille anni, solvetur Satanas de custodia sua, et egredietur ut seducat gentes in quatuor angulis terrae, Gog, et Magog, ut congreget eos ad bellum, quorum numerus est sicut arena maris.
passages.english: The Jews, then, and our own judaizers think that Gog are the Scythian nations, savage and innumerable, which extend beyond the Caucasus mountain and the Maeotic marsh, and near the Caspian sea as far as India; and that after the thousand-year reign these will be stirred up by the devil, to come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, with many nations gathered with them. First Meshech, whom Josephus interprets as Cappadocians; then Tubal, whom the same [interprets as] Iberians, or Spaniards, [and] the Hebrews suppose to be Italians; having with them in the army Persians, Ethiopians and Libyans; Gomer too and Togarmah, whom they interpret as Galatians and Phrygians; Sabaeans also and Dedan, and Carthaginians, or Tarshish. And this is what John too sets down in his Apocalypse: "And when the thousand years are finished, Satan will be loosed from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for war, whose number is as the sand of the sea."
passages.notes: The stray "4" after Scythicas is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: Et describes domum et praeparationem ejus, et exitus atque in- troitus ejus, et substantiam ejus et omnia praece- pta illius, et omnia legitima ejus, et omnes leges ejus ostendes illis, et describes coram eis : et cus- todient omnes justificationes et omnia praecepta mea, et facient ea, et descriptionem domus in ver- tice montis, omnes termini ejus in circuitu Sancta sanctorum sunt. Ista est lex domus. » Non parvi operis est, quod oculis carnis, vel mente conspe- xeris audientibus demonstrare, ut et ipsi tecum vidisse videantur. Quamobrem scribit et Josephus, eos qui ad describendam terram missi sunt ab Jesu filio Nave 1, fuisse γεωμέτρας, et artem quae nunc philosophorum propria est, habuisse Geometriae. Domui igitur Israel, eorum qui animo conspiciunt Deum, ostenditur domus, hoc est templum quod Ezechiel situm in monte conspexit, et non solum in monte, sed sicut nunc dicitur, in summitate montis : quam nequaquam illam putemus, quae a Salomone constructa narratur in Regum et in Paralipomenon libris.
passages.english: "And you shall describe the house and its arrangement, and its exits and entrances, and its substance and all its precepts, and all its ordinances, and you shall show them all its laws, and describe them before them; and they shall keep all my judgements and all my precepts and do them; and the description of the house on the top of the mountain: all its boundaries round about are the Holy of holies. This is the law of the house." It is no small labour to show to hearers what you have seen with the eyes of the flesh or with the mind, so that they too seem to have seen it with you. For this reason Josephus also writes that those who were sent by Joshua son of Nun to describe the land were geometers, and had the art of geometry, which is now peculiar to the philosophers. To the house of Israel, then, of those who behold God with the mind, the house is shown, that is, the temple which Ezekiel saw set on a mountain, and not only on a mountain but, as is now said, on the summit of the mountain: which we should by no means think to be the one that is narrated in the books of Kings and Chronicles as built by Solomon.
passages.notes: The lemma's syntax ("et descriptionem domus...") is loose in the Latin; rendered literally.

passages.original: XXVII, 25), et, Velum templi scissum est, et omnia Hebraeorum sacramenta reserata, respon- derunt praecipienti Domino, atque dixerunt : Cu- ravimus Babylonem, et non est sanata : relinqua- mus eam (Jerem.LI, 9), urbem videlicet confusionis atque vitiorum. Unde et Josephus in sua narrat Historia, quod postquam Dominus crucifixus est, et velum templi scissum est, sive liminare templi fractum corruit, audita sit vox 1 in adytis templi virtutum coelestium, Transeamus ex his sedibus.
passages.english: (Matt. 27:25), and the veil of the temple was torn, and all the mysteries of the Hebrews laid open, they answered the Lord's command and said: "We have treated Babylon, and she is not healed; let us leave her" (Jer. 51:9), that is, the city of confusion and vices. Hence Josephus too narrates in his History that after the Lord was crucified and the veil of the temple was torn, or the lintel of the temple broke and fell, a voice of the heavenly powers was heard in the inner sanctuary of the temple: "Let us pass from these seats."
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence; the subject (the angels who presided over the Jewish people) is in the preceding context.
